nameStory: The name 'brant' comes from the Old Norse word 'brandgás,' meaning 'burnt goose,' referring to their dark, charcoal-colored plumage that looks like it's been singed by fire. In Europe, they're called 'brent geese,' which shares the same burning etymology. This small, dark goose earned its fiery name from early seafaring peoples who encountered flocks along northern coastlines.
description: The Brant is a compact, dark goose that's much smaller than the familiar Canada Goose you might see on ponds and golf courses. These stocky seabirds are predominantly charcoal-black on their head, neck, and back, with a distinctive white collar marking and pale belly. Adults are about the size of a large duck, making them the smallest of the 'black geese' in their genus. Unlike their freshwater cousins, Brants are true ocean birds that spend most of their time along saltwater coastlines.

idTips.label: White neck collar
idTips.description: Look for a broken white collar or necklace marking on the dark neck - it appears as white streaks or patches that don't completely circle the neck, like a fancy but incomplete choker necklace

idTips.label: Compact size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than Canada Geese, about the size of a Mallard duck, with a stocky, rounded body that sits low on the water like a floating football

idTips.label: Dark head and neck
idTips.description: Head and neck are deep charcoal-black or dark brown, much darker than a Canada Goose, appearing almost sooty in bright sunlight

idTips.label: Pale belly contrast
idTips.description: Light gray to whitish belly creates a sharp contrast with the dark upper parts, visible even when the bird is swimming

idTips.label: Coastal behavior
idTips.description: Almost always found in salt water or nearby coastal areas, feeding in shallow water by tipping forward like a dabbling duck

habitat: Brants are strictly coastal birds in New England, found along salt marshes, shallow bays, estuaries, and rocky shorelines from Maine to Connecticut. They prefer areas with eelgrass beds and sea lettuce, their favorite foods, and are most common in protected waters like Plum Island Sound in Massachusetts or the Connecticut River estuary. Unlike other geese, you'll never find them on freshwater ponds or inland areas.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs from March through May as flocks move north to Arctic breeding grounds. Look for large rafts of hundreds of birds in coastal waters, often mixed with other waterfowl.
seasonality.summer: Very rare in New England during summer as they breed on high Arctic tundra. Any summer sightings are likely non-breeding birds or stragglers.
seasonality.fall: Return migration begins in September and peaks in October-November. This is often the best time to observe them as they gather in large flocks to feed before continuing south.
seasonality.winter: Common winter residents along the coast, especially in Massachusetts and Connecticut. They form large flocks that can be seen floating offshore or feeding in shallow coastal waters during low tide.

funFact: A major oil field in the North Sea was named 'Brent' after this little goose because Shell's policy was to name oilfields after birds, and the Brent Goose was the first bird name starting with 'B' that came up in their alphabetical naming system - making this humble seabird inadvertently famous in the energy industry!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with Canada Geese, but Brants are much smaller, darker, and always found near salt water. Remember: 'Brants stay briny' - they stick to salt water, while Canada Geese prefer fresh water. The white neck marking on a Brant is broken and streaky, not a solid chinstrap like a Canada Goose.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their small size, Brants make one of the longest migrations of any goose, traveling from Arctic Canada to wintering grounds as far south as Mexico. Their dependence on eelgrass nearly caused their extinction in the 1930s when a disease wiped out eelgrass beds, showing how specialized coastal species can be vulnerable to environmental changes.
compareHints: Compared to Canada Geese, Brants are much smaller, darker overall, and have a broken white neck collar instead of a white chinstrap. Unlike the large, honking Canada Goose, Brants make softer, rolling calls and are strictly coastal birds. Cackling Geese are closer in size but have the white chinstrap pattern of Canada Geese and aren't typically found in saltwater environments.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canada Geese are much larger and more common than their relatives in New England.
Compared to Canada geese, cackling geese are significantly smaller with proportionally shorter necks and rounder heads.

Among the black geese, barnacle geese are the only ones with extensive white on the face - Canada geese have white chin straps, brant have small white neck patches, and cackling geese look like mini Canada geese.
